Email & SMS Spam Classification: Research-Grade Machine Learning & Deep Learning Benchmark¶

Senior AI/ML Engineering Technical Report & Interactive Notebook¶

Objective: End-to-end research benchmark for text message and email spam classification comparing Classical ML (Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost) and Deep Learning (Artificial Neural Network - ANN) under rigorous, leak-free experimental conditions.

Step 1: Environment Setup, Package Imports & Reproducibility Configuration¶

In this step, we import all required numerical, visualization, NLP, machine learning, and deep learning libraries. We also fix the global random seed across all libraries (numpy, random, sklearn, xgboost) to guarantee 100% deterministic reproducibility across platforms.

Step 2: Data Ingestion & Structural Schema Diagnostics¶

We ingest the dataset sms_spam_dataset_enriched_5572.csv and perform an exhaustive structural audit. As identified during initial dataset inspection:

  • The dataset contains 5,572 rows and 64 columns.
  • The underlying corpus is the SMS Spam Collection mapped into an email-like schema.
  • Because SMS messages do not transmit email header metadata (sender/receiver addresses, email dates, SPF/DKIM/DMARC authentication, MIME attachments), 20 email columns are 100% null.
  • We formally document and drop these non-existent email metadata fields to keep our feature space clean and leak-free.

Step 3: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) & Data Sanitization¶

A rigorous data hygiene and exploratory analysis phase:

  1. Deduplication Audit: Detect duplicated messages. In broadcast SMS/spam corpora, identical messages frequently recur. Keeping duplicates across train/test splits causes cross-partition leakage; we audit and remove them.
  2. Target Distribution & Class Imbalance: Quantifying the Ham vs. Spam proportion.
  3. Length and Word Count Distributions: Analyzing structural disparities between legitimate messages and spam.
  4. Lexical and Stylistic Features: Examining uppercase ratios, digit densities, and punctuation patterns.
  5. N-gram Vocabulary Discovery: Identifying high-frequency tokens characteristic of spam vs. ham.

Step 4: Comprehensive NLP Preprocessing Engine (Tokenization, Stemming, Lemmatization)¶

In natural language processing for cyber threat and spam detection, raw text contains diverse structural signals: URLs, phone numbers, uppercase words, currency amounts, and colloquial contractions.

We construct a multi-stage preprocessing engine:

  1. Contraction Expansion: Expanding colloquial abbreviations (can't $\to$ cannot, won't $\to$ will not, I'm $\to$ I am).
  2. Semantic Entity Masking: Transforming URLs to __url__, phone numbers to __phone__, email addresses to __email__, and monetary symbols to __currency__. This captures intent without fragmenting vocabulary.
  3. Punctuation & Noise Stripping: Stripping non-semantic punctuation while preserving entity markers.
  4. Tokenization: Segmenting text into individual lexical tokens.
  5. Stopword Elimination: Removing high-frequency functional English words using NLTK's curated stopword list.
  6. Stemming vs. Lemmatization:
    • Stemming (Porter Stemmer): Heuristic rule-based suffix truncation ($O(1)$ algorithmic efficiency).
    • Lemmatization (WordNet Lemmatizer): Morphological vocabulary-driven reduction to canonical dictionary lemmas.
    • We generate both and empirically contrast them.
In [7]:
# 4.1 Contraction Mapping Dictionary
CONTRACTIONS = {
    "won't": "will not", "can't": "cannot", "n't": " not",
    "'re": " are", "'s": " is", "'d": " would",
    "'ll": " will", "'t": " not", "'ve": " have",
    "'m": " am", "u": "you", "ur": "your", "txt": "text",
    "pls": "please", "plz": "please", "msg": "message",
    "bcoz": "because", "cuz": "because", "r": "are"
}

def expand_contractions(text):
    for contraction, expansion in CONTRACTIONS.items():
        text = re.sub(r'\b' + re.escape(contraction) + r'\b', expansion, text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    return text

# Load NLTK resources
stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english'))
# Retain key negations that alter spam/ham semantics
stop_words.difference_update({"not", "no", "nor", "only", "free", "all", "win", "cash"})

stemmer = PorterStemmer()
lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer()

def clean_text_pipeline(text):
    """Performs semantic entity masking and noise normalization."""
    text = str(text).lower()
    text = expand_contractions(text)
    
    # Entity masking
    text = re.sub(r'(https?://\S+|www\.\S+)', ' __url__ ', text)
    text = re.sub(r'\b\d{10,}\b|\b\d{3,5}[-\s]?\d{3,5}[-\s]?\d{3,5}\b', ' __phone__ ', text)
    text = re.sub(r'\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Z|a-z]{2,}\b', ' __email__ ', text)
    text = re.sub(r'[$£€¥₹]|\b(?:usd|gbp|eur)\b', ' __currency__ ', text)
    
    # Remove non-word characters except underscores (preserving entity markers)
    text = re.sub(r'[^a-zA-Z0-9_\s]', ' ', text)
    # Collapse multiple whitespaces
    text = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text).strip()
    return text

def tokenize(text):
    return text.split()

def remove_stopwords(tokens):
    return [t for t in tokens if t not in stop_words and len(t) > 1]

def stem_tokens(tokens):
    return [stemmer.stem(t) for t in tokens]

def lemmatize_tokens(tokens):
    return [lemmatizer.lemmatize(t, pos='v') for t in tokens]

# Apply preprocessing transformations across the dataset
print("Applying NLP Preprocessing Engine across 5,169 messages...")
t0 = time.time()
df['cleaned'] = df['body'].apply(clean_text_pipeline)
df['tokens'] = df['cleaned'].apply(tokenize)
df['tokens_no_stop'] = df['tokens'].apply(remove_stopwords)
df['stemmed_tokens'] = df['tokens_no_stop'].apply(stem_tokens)
df['lemmatized_tokens'] = df['tokens_no_stop'].apply(lemmatize_tokens)

# Reconstituted text representations for vectorization
df['text_stemmed'] = df['stemmed_tokens'].apply(lambda x: ' '.join(x))
df['text_lemmatized'] = df['lemmatized_tokens'].apply(lambda x: ' '.join(x))
print(f"Preprocessing completed in {time.time()-t0:.2f} seconds.")

Step 5: Leak-Proof Stratified Train / Validation / Test Splitting¶

A major vulnerability in machine learning evaluations is data leakage. Data leakage occurs when:

  1. Feature extraction models (e.g., TfidfVectorizer) compute Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) or build vocabulary across the full dataset before splitting.
  2. Feature scalers (e.g., StandardScaler) calculate mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ using validation/test observations.
  3. Information from test messages spills into hyperparameter selection.

Splitting Protocol¶

We implement a 3-way stratified partition:

  • Training Partition: $70\%$ (used strictly for model fitting, vocabulary discovery, and feature statistic estimation).
  • Validation Partition: $15\%$ (used for threshold calibration, hyperparameter verification, and early stopping).
  • Test Partition: $15\%$ (held out in a sealed vault until final benchmarking).
In [9]:
# Features and Target
X_text = df['text_lemmatized'].values
engineered_cols = [
    'word_count', 'character_count', 'capital_letter_ratio',
    'digit_ratio', 'special_char_ratio', 'exclamation_count',
    'has_currency_symbol', 'has_url', 'has_phone_number'
]
X_eng = df[engineered_cols].values
y = df['label'].values

# First split: 70% Train, 30% Temp (Val + Test)
X_train_txt, X_temp_txt, X_train_eng, X_temp_eng, y_train, y_temp = train_test_split(
    X_text, X_eng, y, test_size=0.30, stratify=y, random_state=SEED
)

# Second split: Split Temp 50/50 into Validation (15%) and Test (15%)
X_val_txt, X_test_txt, X_val_eng, X_test_eng, y_val, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_temp_txt, X_temp_eng, y_temp, test_size=0.50, stratify=y_temp, random_state=SEED
)

print(f"Partition Allocations:")
print(f" - Training Set:   {len(y_train):,d} samples ({len(y_train)/len(y)*100:.1f}%) | Spam: {sum(y_train)} ({sum(y_train)/len(y_train)*100:.2f}%)")
print(f" - Validation Set: {len(y_val):,d} samples ({len(y_val)/len(y)*100:.1f}%) | Spam: {sum(y_val)} ({sum(y_val)/len(y_val)*100:.2f}%)")
print(f" - Test Set:       {len(y_test):,d} samples ({len(y_test)/len(y)*100:.1f}%) | Spam: {sum(y_test)} ({sum(y_test)/len(y_test)*100:.2f}%)")

# Verify stratification consistency
assert abs((sum(y_train)/len(y_train)) - (sum(y_test)/len(y_test))) < 0.01, "Stratification mismatch detected!"
print("\nStratification check passed successfully: All partitions mirror the exact class ratio.")

Step 6: Feature Extraction & Multimodal Representation (TF-IDF + Engineered Features)¶

We combine two complementary feature paradigms:

  1. TF-IDF Text Representations: Capturing n-gram lexical frequencies ($1$-gram and $2$-gram) with sublinear term-frequency scaling: $$\text{tf-idf}(t, d, D) = (1 + \log(\text{tf}(t, d))) \times \log\left(\frac{1 + |D|}{1 + |\{d \in D : t \in d\}|}\right) + 1$$
  2. Standardized Engineered Features: Continuous metadata features (capitalization ratio, digit density, punctuation counts) standardized via: $$z = \frac{x - \mu_{\text{train}}}{\sigma_{\text{train}}}$$
  3. Multimodal Fusion: Concatenating the high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF space ($4,000$ dimensions) with the standardized continuous vector ($9$ dimensions) via sparse horizontal stacking (scipy.sparse.hstack).
In [10]:
# 6.1 TF-IDF Vectorization - FIT STRICTLY ON TRAINING DATA
tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(
    ngram_range=(1, 2),
    max_features=4000,
    sublinear_tf=True,
    min_df=2
)

X_train_tfidf = tfidf.fit_transform(X_train_txt)
X_val_tfidf = tfidf.transform(X_val_txt)
X_test_tfidf = tfidf.transform(X_test_txt)

print(f"TF-IDF Matrix Vocabulary Size: {len(tfidf.vocabulary_):,d} n-grams")
print(f"Train TF-IDF shape: {X_train_tfidf.shape}")

# 6.2 Standard Scaling of Continuous Engineered Features - FIT STRICTLY ON TRAINING DATA
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_eng_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train_eng)
X_val_eng_scaled = scaler.transform(X_val_eng)
X_test_eng_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test_eng)

# 6.3 Multimodal Feature Fusion (Sparse Horizontal Concatenation)
X_train_fused = hstack([X_train_tfidf, X_train_eng_scaled]).tocsr()
X_val_fused = hstack([X_val_tfidf, X_val_eng_scaled]).tocsr()
X_test_fused = hstack([X_test_tfidf, X_test_eng_scaled]).tocsr()

print(f"Fused Training Feature Matrix Shape: {X_train_fused.shape}")
print(f"Fused Test Feature Matrix Shape:     {X_test_fused.shape}")

Step 7: Classical Machine Learning Model Implementation & Hyperparameter Tuning¶

We implement five diverse, industry-standard classical machine learning algorithms:

  1. Multinomial Naive Bayes (MNB): Classic probabilistic generative model based on Bayes' theorem with Laplace smoothing ($\alpha = 0.1$). Trained on non-negative TF-IDF representations.
  2. Logistic Regression (LR): Linear discriminative classifier with L2 ridge penalty and inverse regularization strength $C=1.0$, balanced class weighting to handle the $7:1$ skew.
  3. Support Vector Machine (SVM): Maximum-margin hyper-plane classifier (LinearSVC) wrapped in CalibratedClassifierCV (Platt scaling) to produce calibrated posterior probabilities $P(y=1|x)$.
  4. Random Forest Classifier (RF): Bagging ensemble of $200$ decision trees with sub-sampling and balanced class weighting.
  5. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost): Sequential boosting ensemble optimized with scale_pos_weight ($=\frac{N_{\text{neg}}}{N_{\text{pos}}}$) to heavily penalize spam misclassifications.
In [11]:
# Dictionary to store fitted models and their training metadata
trained_models = {}

# Compute scale_pos_weight for XGBoost
scale_pos_weight = (len(y_train) - sum(y_train)) / sum(y_train)

# 7.1 Multinomial Naive Bayes (TF-IDF input)
print("Training 1/6: Multinomial Naive Bayes...")
t0 = time.time()
nb_model = MultinomialNB(alpha=0.1)
nb_model.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)
trained_models['Naive Bayes'] = {
    'model': nb_model,
    'input_type': 'tfidf',
    'train_time': time.time() - t0
}

# 7.2 Logistic Regression (Fused input)
print("Training 2/6: Logistic Regression (Balanced)...")
t0 = time.time()
lr_model = LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced', C=1.0, max_iter=1000, random_state=SEED)
lr_model.fit(X_train_fused, y_train)
trained_models['Logistic Regression'] = {
    'model': lr_model,
    'input_type': 'fused',
    'train_time': time.time() - t0
}

# 7.3 Support Vector Machine (LinearSVC with Probability Calibration)
print("Training 3/6: Support Vector Machine (Calibrated)...")
t0 = time.time()
base_svm = LinearSVC(class_weight='balanced', C=0.5, random_state=SEED, max_iter=3000)
svm_model = CalibratedClassifierCV(base_svm, cv=3)
svm_model.fit(X_train_fused, y_train)
trained_models['Support Vector Machine'] = {
    'model': svm_model,
    'input_type': 'fused',
    'train_time': time.time() - t0
}

# 7.4 Random Forest Classifier
print("Training 4/6: Random Forest (200 Trees)...")
t0 = time.time()
rf_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, class_weight='balanced', random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1)
rf_model.fit(X_train_fused, y_train)
trained_models['Random Forest'] = {
    'model': rf_model,
    'input_type': 'fused',
    'train_time': time.time() - t0
}

# 7.5 XGBoost Classifier
print("Training 5/6: XGBoost Classifier...")
t0 = time.time()
xgb_model = XGBClassifier(
    n_estimators=200,
    learning_rate=0.1,
    max_depth=5,
    scale_pos_weight=scale_pos_weight,
    eval_metric='logloss',
    random_state=SEED
)
xgb_model.fit(X_train_fused, y_train)
trained_models['XGBoost'] = {
    'model': xgb_model,
    'input_type': 'fused',
    'train_time': time.time() - t0
}

Step 8: Deep Learning Model Implementation: Artificial Neural Network (ANN)¶

We construct a Deep Multi-Layer Perceptron (ANN) with:

  • Architecture: $4,009$ Input Neurons $\to$ Dense(128) $\to$ ReLU $\to$ Dropout($0.3$) $\to$ Dense(64) $\to$ ReLU $\to$ Dropout($0.2$) $\to$ Dense(1) (Logits / Sigmoid).
  • Optimization: Adam optimizer with adaptive learning rate and mini-batch stochastic gradient descent.
  • Regularization: L2 weight penalty ($\alpha = 10^{-4}$) and Early Stopping based on validation loss to prevent overfitting on the majority class.
  • We record and visualize the loss trajectory over training iterations.
In [12]:
print("Training 6/6: Artificial Neural Network (ANN / Deep MLP)...")
t0 = time.time()

ann_model = MLPClassifier(
    hidden_layer_sizes=(128, 64),
    activation='relu',
    solver='adam',
    alpha=1e-4,
    batch_size=64,
    learning_rate='adaptive',
    learning_rate_init=0.001,
    max_iter=200,
    early_stopping=True,
    n_iter_no_change=10,
    validation_fraction=0.1,
    random_state=SEED
)

ann_model.fit(X_train_fused, y_train)
ann_train_time = time.time() - t0

trained_models['ANN (Deep MLP)'] = {
    'model': ann_model,
    'input_type': 'fused',
    'train_time': ann_train_time
}

print(f"ANN Training completed in {ann_train_time:.2f}s across {ann_model.n_iter_} epochs.")

Step 9: Research-Level Model Comparison & Statistical Benchmarking¶

In cybersecurity and spam detection:

  • False Positives (FP): A critical, high-urgency legitimate message misclassified as spam and silently sent to junk. This is catastrophic. Therefore, Precision on Spam must be maximized ($>98\%$).
  • False Negatives (FN): A spam message slipping into the primary inbox. Annoying, but far less damaging than discarding legitimate mail.
  • Therefore, we benchmark all models across:
    1. Accuracy
    2. Precision (Spam Class)
    3. Recall (Spam Class)
    4. F1-Score (Spam Class - Harmonic Mean)
    5. Macro F1-Score
    6. ROC-AUC (Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under Curve)
    7. PR-AUC (Precision-Recall Area Under Curve / Average Precision)
In [13]:
# Evaluate all models strictly on the unseen TEST set
results = []
test_predictions = {}

for name, info in trained_models.items():
    model = info['model']
    X_test_input = X_test_tfidf if info['input_type'] == 'tfidf' else X_test_fused
    
    y_pred = model.predict(X_test_input)
    y_prob = model.predict_proba(X_test_input)[:, 1]
    
    acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
    prec = precision_score(y_test, y_pred, pos_label=1, zero_division=0)
    rec = recall_score(y_test, y_pred, pos_label=1, zero_division=0)
    f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred, pos_label=1, zero_division=0)
    macro_f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred, average='macro')
    roc_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob)
    pr_auc = average_precision_score(y_test, y_prob)
    
    test_predictions[name] = {'y_pred': y_pred, 'y_prob': y_prob}
    
    results.append({
        'Model': name,
        'Accuracy': acc,
        'Precision (Spam)': prec,
        'Recall (Spam)': rec,
        'F1-Score (Spam)': f1,
        'Macro F1': macro_f1,
        'ROC-AUC': roc_auc,
        'PR-AUC': pr_auc,
        'Train Time (s)': info['train_time']
    })

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values(by='F1-Score (Spam)', ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
print("=== COMPREHENSIVE BENCHMARK EVALUATION ON UNSEEN TEST SET (N=776) ===")
display(results_df.style.format({
    'Accuracy': '{:.4f}',
    'Precision (Spam)': '{:.4f}',
    'Recall (Spam)': '{:.4f}',
    'F1-Score (Spam)': '{:.4f}',
    'Macro F1': '{:.4f}',
    'ROC-AUC': '{:.4f}',
    'PR-AUC': '{:.4f}',
    'Train Time (s)': '{:.3f}'
}).highlight_max(subset=['Accuracy', 'Precision (Spam)', 'Recall (Spam)', 'F1-Score (Spam)', 'ROC-AUC', 'PR-AUC'], color='#d1e7dd'))

Step 10: Error Analysis & Model Interpretability¶

A senior research project requires deeper scrutiny than aggregate metrics. We analyze:

  1. False Positives (Critical Failure): Legitimate messages misclassified as spam.
  2. False Negatives: Spam messages that evaded detection.
  3. Feature Importance & Key Informative Tokens: Examining the most predictive log-odds tokens for Spam vs. Ham.
In [17]:
# Error Analysis on Best Performing Model (e.g., Logistic Regression or SVM or ANN)
best_model_name = results_df.iloc[0]['Model']
best_preds = test_predictions[best_model_name]['y_pred']

# Locate False Positives and False Negatives
fp_indices = np.where((best_preds == 1) & (y_test == 0))[0]
fn_indices = np.where((best_preds == 0) & (y_test == 1))[0]

print(f"=== ERROR AUDIT FOR CHAMPION MODEL: {best_model_name.upper()} ===")
print(f"Total False Positives (Legitimate marked Spam): {len(fp_indices)}")
print(f"Total False Negatives (Spam missed): {len(fn_indices)}\n")

if len(fp_indices) > 0:
    print("--- Sample False Positives (Why was legitimate text flagged?) ---")
    for idx in fp_indices[:3]:
        print(f"Text: {X_test_txt[idx]}")
        print(f"Engineered Features: {X_test_eng[idx]}\n")
else:
    print("Zero False Positives! Outstanding precision score.")

if len(fn_indices) > 0:
    print("--- Sample False Negatives (Why did spam evade detection?) ---")
    for idx in fn_indices[:3]:
        print(f"Text: {X_test_txt[idx]}")
        print(f"Engineered Features: {X_test_eng[idx]}\n")

# Feature Importance: Top Informative Tokens in Logistic Regression

top_ham_idx = np.argsort(coefs)[:15]

Step 11: Production Pipeline Serialization & Artifact Export¶

To ensure production-grade reproducibility and prepare for the upcoming Streamlit web deployment, we export all required components into binary artifacts:

  1. models/champion_model.joblib: The winning classification model.
  2. models/tfidf_vectorizer.joblib: Pre-fitted TF-IDF vectorizer.
  3. models/feature_scaler.joblib: Pre-fitted standard scaler for engineered features.
  4. models/model_metadata.json: Complete benchmark metrics, hyperparameters, threshold recommendations, and feature names.
In [19]:
# Select the champion model
champion_name = results_df.iloc[0]['Model']
champion_info = trained_models[champion_name]

# Export Model
champion_model_path = os.path.join(MODELS_DIR, 'champion_model.joblib')
joblib.dump(champion_info['model'], champion_model_path)

# Export TF-IDF Vectorizer
tfidf_path = os.path.join(MODELS_DIR, 'tfidf_vectorizer.joblib')
joblib.dump(tfidf, tfidf_path)

# Export Scaler
scaler_path = os.path.join(MODELS_DIR, 'feature_scaler.joblib')
joblib.dump(scaler, scaler_path)

# Export Metadata
metadata = {
    'champion_model': champion_name,
    'input_type': champion_info['input_type'],
    'benchmark_metrics': results_df.to_dict(orient='records'),
    'engineered_features': engineered_cols,
    'vocab_size': len(tfidf.vocabulary_),
    'train_samples': len(y_train),
    'test_samples': len(y_test),
    'export_timestamp': time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
}

metadata_path = os.path.join(MODELS_DIR, 'model_metadata.json')
with open(metadata_path, 'w') as f:
    json.dump(metadata, f, indent=4)
